newsitem.title: BRAZIL: W. Europe OJ demand seen growing 3-5 pct per year.
newsitem.headline: W. Europe OJ demand seen growing 3-5 pct per year.

text.p: Western European consumption of orange juice concentrates should grow three to five percent annually over the next 10 years, said the president of the Brazilian Association of Citrus Exporters (Abecitrus).

"We can see no reason why Western Europe...cannot maintain an annual consumption growth of three to five percent over the next decade," said Ademerval Garcia in a speech to the Citrus Economists' Meeting in New Orleans on October 29.

Average annual growth in orange concentrate use was close to six percent over the last 10 years, slowing down to below four percent in the last three years after reaching almost 10 percent shortly after German reunification.

Amongst individual countries, annual per capita consumption of all fruit juices and nectars varies from a low of 3.5 liters in Portugal to 42 liters in Germany, with average per capita consumption in Western Europe around 20 liters.

Orange juice and orange nectars represent more than half of this volume and of the one million tonnes plus of 65 brix equivalent FCOJ consumed in Western Europe, about 70 percent comes from Brazil, Garcia said.
The Japanese market, which is going to play a major role in the world juice business, is growing more slowly than most expected, he added.
Japan currently consumes about 140,000 tonnes of 65 brix equivalent of FCOJ, including approximately 30,000 tonnes of domestic Mikan juice production.
By the year 2000 this market may exceed the 200,000 tonnes level but four years ago the industry had expected to have passed this mark by now.
South Korea is the second largest market in the Pacific Rim, consuming over 60,000 tonnes of FCOJ, most of which comes from Brazil under an import quota system.
After July 1997, orange juice imports will be liberalised and it is likely that consumption in Korea will still grow at double digit rates for a number of years.
North America, Western Europe, Japan and Korea are the dominant consumer markets of today and will continue to be the important backbone to Brazilian business.
But Eastern Europe, Russia and other countries of the former Soviet Union, while currently only consuming small amounts of orange juice, present extraordinary potential.

Even though it will take many years before purchasing power has risen enough for Eastern Europeans to consume more of what for them may be a luxury product, their markets have more than doubled in the last five years.
Over the next few years, it will be in the European and Far Eastern markets where Brazilian sales will make up for the volume lost in North America, Garcia said.
This will allow Brazil to maintain annual shipments of around 1.1 million tonnes until the demand curve for Brazilian FCOJ points up again, probably by the turn of the century, he added.
-- Caroline Bulloch, Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151
